title: Welcome To My Blog
text:
Welcome! This blog is where I write up things I’m exploring in math, statistics, and machine learning — usually starting from a paper or an idea I want to understand better, and working through it in code until it’s concrete.
Expect a mix of interactive explainers, reproductions of results from papers I find interesting, and the occasional deep dive into a dataset or method. Posts will lean toward showing the work rather than just stating conclusions, so there’s often code, data, and plots alongside the writing.

Thanks for stopping by — more soon.

title: RG Functional Equations & Critical Phenomena
text:
The paper considers the subject of critical phenomena in the physical world of thermodynamics and its analog in the economic world and the formation of bubbles in financial markets. Providing a review and comparison of a “bottom-up” approach based on statistical mechanics with a more “top-down” construction using iterative solutions to functional equations, both of which exhibit the required scale invariance (power laws) and fractal qualities seen near the critical points, and where the renormalization group theory provides a “bridge” between these two approaches both in a physical and mathematical sense.
M840 Dissertation in Mathematics, The Open University.

title: Projecting the sun’s path for the 12 August 2026 UK partial solar eclipse
text:
Overview
This report projects the sun’s calculated azimuth/altitude path during the 12 August 2026 partial solar eclipse onto two images taken near 52.8936°N, 1.2659°W (Nottinghamshire/Lincolnshire border, UK), and separately visualizes the local terrain to give context on nearby high ground:

A Google Street View image, aimed toward the sun’s position at peak eclipse.
A photo taken with the Theodolite app, whose EXIF/XMP metadata records the camera’s GPS position, compass heading, and pitch.
A 3D terrain surface of the surrounding 10-mile radius, with nearby named hills labeled and the local river network draped over the relief.

Both overlays use the same sun-path calculation and a small-angle (linear) projection from angular offset to pixel offset around the camera’s heading/pitch — not a true perspective projection. This is a reasonable approximation over the modest angular ranges involved here, but it is not exact, especially toward the edges of a wide field of view.

title: Projecting the sun’s path for the 12 August 2026 UK partial solar eclipse
text:
Eclipse context and sun path

lat <- 52.893608
lon <- -1.265934
date <- as.Date("2026-08-12")

# Eclipse locally runs roughly 18:00-20:00 BST (17:00-19:00 UTC);
# widen slightly either side to give context on the sun's path
times <- seq(
  from = as.POSIXct(paste(date, "16:30:00"), tz = "UTC"),
  to   = as.POSIXct(paste(date, "19:15:00"), tz = "UTC"),
  by   = "1 min"
)

sun_path <- getSunlightPosition(date = times, lat = lat, lon = lon) |>
  mutate(
    # Convert azimuth (radians south-to-west) to compass degrees (0-360 from North)
    azimuth_deg = (azimuth * 180 / pi + 180) %% 360,
    altitude_deg = altitude * 180 / pi,
    time_bst = format(with_tz(date, "Europe/London"), "%H:%M")
  )

# Reported UK-wide maximum eclipse is ~19:05-19:13 BST (18:05-18:13 UTC);
# pick the row closest to 19:09 BST (18:09 UTC) for this longitude
peak_time <- as.POSIXct(paste(date, "18:09:00"), tz = "UTC")
peak_sun <- sun_path[which.min(abs(sun_path$date - peak_time)), ]

At peak eclipse (19:09 BST), the sun is at an azimuth of 278.9° and an altitude of 12.1°. Across the wider window shown here (16:30-19:15 UTC / 17:30-20:15 BST), azimuth ranges from 258.9° to 291.7°, and altitude from 2.5° to 27°.
A shared helper converts an azimuth/altitude offset from a camera’s heading/pitch into pixel coordinates, given the image size and field of view:

wrap180 <- function(x) ((x + 180) %% 360) - 180

project_sun <- function(az, alt, heading, pitch, fov_h, fov_v, img_w, img_h) {
  delta_az <- wrap180(az - heading)
  delta_alt <- alt - pitch
  data.frame(
    x = img_w / 2 + (delta_az / (fov_h / 2)) * (img_w / 2),
    y = img_h / 2 + (delta_alt / (fov_v / 2)) * (img_h / 2),
    delta_az = delta_az,
    delta_alt = delta_alt
  )
}

title: Projecting the sun’s path for the 12 August 2026 UK partial solar eclipse
text:
Street View overlay
The Street View camera is pointed toward the sun’s position at peak eclipse (heading 278.9°, pitch 12.1°), using the default 90° horizontal field of view for a square image.

# Cache network responses on disk so repeated re-renders (e.g. while
# iterating on this document) don't repeatedly hit external APIs and risk
# tripping their rate limits.
cache_dir <- ".cache"
dir.create(cache_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

sv_size <- c(640, 640)
sv_fov <- 90
sv_heading <- peak_sun$azimuth_deg
sv_pitch <- peak_sun$altitude_deg

sv_cache_file <- file.path(
  cache_dir,
  sprintf("streetview_%s_%s_h%.1f_p%.1f_f%d_%dx%d.jpg",
          lat, lon, sv_heading, sv_pitch, sv_fov, sv_size[1], sv_size[2])
)

if (!file.exists(sv_cache_file)) {
  api_key <- Sys.getenv("GOOGLE_MAPS_KEY")

  sv_url <- modify_url(
    "https://maps.googleapis.com/maps/api/streetview",
    query = list(
      location = paste(lat, lon, sep = ","),
      size     = paste(sv_size, collapse = "x"),
      heading  = sv_heading,
      fov      = sv_fov,
      pitch    = sv_pitch,
      key      = api_key
    )
  )

  sv_resp <- GET(sv_url, write_disk(sv_cache_file, overwrite = TRUE))
  stop_for_status(sv_resp)
}

streetview_img <- readJPEG(sv_cache_file)


sv_w <- sv_size[1]
sv_h <- sv_size[2]

sv_projected <- cbind(
  sun_path,
  project_sun(sun_path$azimuth_deg, sun_path$altitude_deg,
              sv_heading, sv_pitch, sv_fov, sv_fov, sv_w, sv_h)
) |>
  filter(abs(delta_az) <= sv_fov / 2, abs(delta_alt) <= sv_fov / 2)

sv_peak_projected <- sv_projected |> filter(date == peak_sun$date)


ggplot() +
  annotation_raster(streetview_img, xmin = 0, xmax = sv_w, ymin = 0, ymax = sv_h) +
  geom_path(data = sv_projected, aes(x = x, y = y), color = "yellow", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = sv_peak_projected, aes(x = x, y = y), color = "red", size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = sv_peak_projected, aes(x = x, y = y, label = time_bst),
             color = "red", vjust = -1) +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(0, sv_w), ylim = c(0, sv_h), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Sun's path during the 12 Aug 2026 partial solar eclipse",
    subtitle = paste0("Camera heading ", round(sv_heading, 1), "°, pitch ",
                       round(sv_pitch, 1), "° — near Nottinghamshire/Lincolnshire border"),
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(color = "white"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "white"),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "black")
  )







Figure 1: Sun’s path during the 12 Aug 2026 partial solar eclipse, projected onto a Street View image

title: Projecting the sun’s path for the 12 August 2026 UK partial solar eclipse
text:
Photo overlay
This photo was taken with the Theodolite app on an iPhone, which records GPS position and GPSImgDirection (true compass heading) in EXIF, and the camera’s vertical/horizontal inclination (vert_angle_deg / horiz_angle_deg) in the image caption. We treat vert_angle_deg as pitch and treat roll (horiz_angle_deg) as negligible.

photo_path <- "/Users/paul/Downloads/TH000003.JPG"

meta <- exif_read(photo_path)

Using ExifTool version 13.55

photo_lat <- meta$GPSLatitude
photo_lon <- meta$GPSLongitude
heading   <- meta$GPSImgDirection
pitch     <- as.numeric(sub(".*vert_angle_deg=([0-9.\\-]+).*", "\\1", meta$ImageDescription))

photo_time_local <- as.POSIXct(
  paste(gsub(":", "-", substr(meta$DateTimeOriginal, 1, 10)), substr(meta$DateTimeOriginal, 12, 19)),
  tz = "UTC"
) - hours(as.numeric(substr(meta$OffsetTimeOriginal, 1, 3)))

img_w <- meta$ImageWidth
img_h <- meta$ImageHeight

The photo’s field of view is estimated from its 35mm-equivalent focal length, rescaled to the actual saved crop dimensions assuming the native ultra-wide sensor is 4032x3024 pixels (iPhone 13 Pro Max ultra-wide camera) and a rectilinear (tangent-plane) projection. This is an approximation — the lens’s true optical FOV may differ from this 35mm-equivalent estimate.

native_w <- 4032
f35 <- meta$FocalLengthIn35mmFormat
fov_h_native <- 2 * atan(18 / f35) * 180 / pi
fov_h <- 2 * atan(tan(fov_h_native / 2 * pi / 180) * (img_w / native_w)) * 180 / pi
fov_v <- 2 * atan((img_h / img_w) * tan(fov_h / 2 * pi / 180)) * 180 / pi

Camera heading 279.1°, pitch 2.1°, estimated field of view 87° x 48°, captured 14:08 UTC.

sun_path_photo <- getSunlightPosition(date = times, lat = photo_lat, lon = photo_lon) |>
  mutate(
    azimuth_deg = (azimuth * 180 / pi + 180) %% 360,
    altitude_deg = altitude * 180 / pi,
    time_bst = format(with_tz(date, "Europe/London"), "%H:%M")
  )

capture_sun <- getSunlightPosition(date = photo_time_local, lat = photo_lat, lon = photo_lon) |>
  mutate(
    azimuth_deg = (azimuth * 180 / pi + 180) %% 360,
    altitude_deg = altitude * 180 / pi
  )


sun_projected <- cbind(
  sun_path_photo,
  project_sun(sun_path_photo$azimuth_deg, sun_path_photo$altitude_deg,
              heading, pitch, fov_h, fov_v, img_w, img_h)
)
capture_projected <- cbind(
  capture_sun,
  project_sun(capture_sun$azimuth_deg, capture_sun$altitude_deg,
              heading, pitch, fov_h, fov_v, img_w, img_h)
)

in_frame <- function(x, y) x >= 0 & x <= img_w & y >= 0 & y <= img_h

path_in_frame <- sun_projected |> filter(in_frame(x, y))
capture_in_frame <- in_frame(capture_projected$x[1], capture_projected$y[1])

path_ticks <- path_in_frame |> filter(minute(date) %% 15 == 0)

photo_img <- readJPEG(photo_path)


p_photo <- ggplot() +
  annotation_raster(photo_img, xmin = 0, xmax = img_w, ymin = 0, ymax = img_h) +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(0, img_w), ylim = c(0, img_h), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(
    title = "Eclipse sun path projected onto photo",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Heading ", round(heading, 1), "°, pitch ", round(pitch, 1),
      "°, est. FOV ", round(fov_h, 0), "°x", round(fov_v, 0),
      "°, captured ", format(photo_time_local, "%H:%M UTC")
    ),
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(color = "white", size = 11),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "white", size = 9),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "black")
  )

if (nrow(path_in_frame) > 0) {
  p_photo <- p_photo +
    geom_path(data = path_in_frame, aes(x = x, y = y), color = "yellow", linewidth = 1) +
    geom_point(data = path_ticks, aes(x = x, y = y), color = "yellow", size = 2) +
    geom_label(
      data = path_ticks, aes(x = x, y = y, label = time_bst),
      color = "black", fill = "yellow", alpha = 0.8, size = 2.8,
      linewidth = 0, label.padding = unit(0.12, "lines"), vjust = -0.5
    )
}

if (isTRUE(capture_in_frame)) {
  p_photo <- p_photo +
    geom_point(data = capture_projected, aes(x = x, y = y), color = "red", size = 3) +
    geom_label(data = capture_projected, aes(x = x, y = y, label = "sun at capture"),
               color = "red", fill = "white", alpha = 0.8, linewidth = 0, vjust = -0.7)
} else {
  cx <- pmin(pmax(capture_projected$x, 0), img_w)
  cy <- pmin(pmax(capture_projected$y, 0), img_h)
  offframe_label <- sprintf(
    "Sun at capture (%s) is %.0f° off-frame\n(Az %.0f°, Alt %.0f° vs heading %.0f°, pitch %.0f°)",
    format(photo_time_local, "%H:%M UTC"),
    sqrt(capture_projected$delta_az^2 + capture_projected$delta_alt^2),
    capture_sun$azimuth_deg, capture_sun$altitude_deg, heading, pitch
  )
  p_photo <- p_photo +
    annotate("segment", x = img_w / 2, y = img_h / 2, xend = cx, yend = cy,
             arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm")), color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
    annotate("label", x = img_w * 0.02, y = img_h * 0.02, label = offframe_label,
             color = "red", fill = "white", alpha = 0.85, size = 3, hjust = 0, vjust = 0,
             linewidth = 0)
}

if (nrow(path_in_frame) == 0) {
  p_photo <- p_photo +
    annotate("label", x = img_w * 0.02, y = img_h * 0.98,
             label = "Eclipse sun path (16:30-19:15 UTC) never enters this frame",
             color = "black", fill = "yellow", alpha = 0.85, size = 3, hjust = 0, vjust = 1,
             linewidth = 0)
}

p_photo

section: Terrain and named peaks within 10 miles
text:
Terrain and named peaks within 10 miles
To give context on nearby high ground that could obstruct a low-altitude view of the eclipse, this section builds a 3D terrain surface for a 10-mile radius around the viewing location and labels the named hills found in OpenStreetMap within that area.

miles_to_deg_lat <- 10 / 69.0
miles_to_deg_lon <- 10 / (69.0 * cos(lat * pi / 180))

bbox_sf <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(
    lon = c(lon - miles_to_deg_lon, lon + miles_to_deg_lon),
    lat = c(lat - miles_to_deg_lat, lat + miles_to_deg_lat)
  ),
  coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326
)

# Cache as a GeoTIFF (rather than saveRDS) so the raster's values are
# guaranteed to round-trip regardless of in-memory vs. file-backed state.
elev_cache_file <- file.path(
  cache_dir, sprintf("elev_raster_%s_%s_z10.tif", lat, lon)
)

if (file.exists(elev_cache_file)) {
  elev_raster <- raster::raster(elev_cache_file)
} else {
  elev_raster <- get_elev_raster(bbox_sf, z = 10, src = "aws")
  raster::writeRaster(elev_raster, elev_cache_file, overwrite = TRUE)
}

# Reproject to British National Grid so grid cells are isotropic (equal
# distance in x and y), which raw lat/lon degrees are not at this latitude
r_bng <- terra::project(terra::rast(elev_raster), "EPSG:27700", method = "bilinear", res = 30)


# osmdata's default Overpass mirror can vary and has been observed rate-
# limiting/blocking repeated requests from this machine (surfacing as a
# 429/420-style error after a long retry backoff). Pin to the main
# overpass-api.de instance, which has been confirmed reachable.
set_overpass_url("https://overpass-api.de/api/interpreter")

bbox_num <- c(lon - miles_to_deg_lon, lat - miles_to_deg_lat, lon + miles_to_deg_lon, lat + miles_to_deg_lat)

peaks_cache_file <- file.path(cache_dir, sprintf("osm_peaks_%s_%s.rds", lat, lon))

if (file.exists(peaks_cache_file)) {
  peaks <- readRDS(peaks_cache_file)
} else {
  peaks <- opq(bbox = bbox_num, timeout = 120) |>
    add_osm_feature(key = "natural", value = "peak") |>
    osmdata_sf()
  saveRDS(peaks, peaks_cache_file)
}

peak_named <- peaks$osm_points |> filter(!is.na(name))

peak_named_bng <- st_transform(peak_named, 27700)
peak_coords <- st_coordinates(peak_named_bng)

peak_df <- data.frame(
  name = peak_named_bng$name,
  easting = peak_coords[, "X"],
  northing = peak_coords[, "Y"]
) |>
  distinct(name, .keep_all = TRUE)

# Look up each peak's elevation from the DEM rather than relying on
# (frequently missing) OSM elevation tags
peak_df$elev_dem <- terra::extract(r_bng, as.matrix(peak_df[, c("easting", "northing")]))[, 1]
peak_df <- peak_df |> arrange(desc(elev_dem))

top_peaks <- head(peak_df, 8)

# The eclipse-viewing location itself (Long Eaton), for reference on the map
viewing_point_bng <- st_transform(st_sfc(st_point(c(lon, lat)), crs = 4326), 27700)
viewing_coords <- st_coordinates(viewing_point_bng)
viewing_point <- data.frame(
  name = "Long Eaton",
  easting = viewing_coords[, "X"],
  northing = viewing_coords[, "Y"]
)
viewing_point$elev_dem <- terra::extract(r_bng, viewing_coords)[, 1]

# The DEM's highest point can sit outside any *named* OSM peak - here it's
# ~25km from the nearest tagged peak (Drum Hill), so it's real high ground
# (likely Peak District/Pennine foothills at the edge of the 10-mile-radius
# bounding box, whose corners reach ~14 miles out) rather than an OSM gap
dem_vals <- terra::values(r_bng)[, 1]
dem_xy <- terra::xyFromCell(r_bng, seq_along(dem_vals))
max_idx <- which.max(dem_vals)
high_point <- data.frame(
  name = "Unnamed high ground",
  easting = dem_xy[max_idx, 1],
  northing = dem_xy[max_idx, 2],
  elev_dem = dem_vals[max_idx]
)

Within this radius, 15 named hills are tagged in OpenStreetMap, ranging from 27 m to 186 m; the eight highest are labeled below, along with the eclipse-viewing location (Long Eaton, at the centre) and the single highest point in the DEM overall (381 m), which falls outside the named-peaks dataset and sits at the edge of the frame.

# NOTE: raster_to_matrix() transposes the raster - its first matrix
# dimension indexes eastings (raster columns), its second indexes
# northings (raster rows, north-to-south)
elmat <- raster_to_matrix(r_bng)

ext_bng <- terra::ext(r_bng)
eastings_full <- seq(ext_bng[1], ext_bng[2], length.out = ncol(r_bng))
northings_full <- seq(ext_bng[4], ext_bng[3], length.out = nrow(r_bng))

# Downsample for a responsive interactive plot
step <- 3
i_seq <- seq(1, nrow(elmat), by = step)
j_seq <- seq(1, ncol(elmat), by = step)
elmat_ds <- elmat[i_seq, j_seq]
eastings_ds <- eastings_full[i_seq]
northings_ds <- northings_full[j_seq]

# plotly's z matrix rows -> y axis, cols -> x axis
z_mat <- t(elmat_ds)


peak_hover <- sprintf("%s<br>%d m", top_peaks$name, round(top_peaks$elev_dem))
viewing_hover <- sprintf("%s<br>%d m", viewing_point$name, round(viewing_point$elev_dem))
high_point_hover <- sprintf("%s<br>%d m", high_point$name, round(high_point$elev_dem))

plot_ly() |>
  add_surface(x = eastings_ds, y = northings_ds, z = z_mat,
              colorscale = "Earth", showscale = FALSE) |>
  add_trace(
    type = "scatter3d", mode = "markers+text",
    x = top_peaks$easting, y = top_peaks$northing, z = top_peaks$elev_dem + 15,
    text = top_peaks$name, textposition = "top center",
    marker = list(color = "red", size = 4),
    textfont = list(color = "black", size = 11),
    hovertext = peak_hover, hoverinfo = "text",
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  add_trace(
    type = "scatter3d", mode = "markers+text",
    x = viewing_point$easting, y = viewing_point$northing, z = viewing_point$elev_dem + 15,
    text = viewing_point$name, textposition = "top center",
    marker = list(color = "blue", size = 5, symbol = "diamond"),
    textfont = list(color = "black", size = 11),
    hovertext = viewing_hover, hoverinfo = "text",
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  add_trace(
    type = "scatter3d", mode = "markers+text",
    x = high_point$easting, y = high_point$northing, z = high_point$elev_dem + 15,
    text = high_point$name, textposition = "top center",
    marker = list(color = "darkorange", size = 4),
    textfont = list(color = "black", size = 11),
    hovertext = high_point_hover, hoverinfo = "text",
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  layout(
    title = "Terrain within 10 miles of the eclipse-viewing location",
    scene = list(
      xaxis = list(title = "Easting (m, BNG)"),
      yaxis = list(title = "Northing (m, BNG)"),
      zaxis = list(title = "Elevation (m)"),
      aspectmode = "manual",
      aspectratio = list(x = 1, y = diff(range(northings_ds)) / diff(range(eastings_ds)), z = 0.25)
    )
  )

title: Projecting the sun’s path for the 12 August 2026 UK partial solar eclipse
text:
River network and 3D rendering
To add geographic context beyond bare terrain, the local river/canal network is draped over a full-resolution rayshader hillshade and rendered as a 3D scene. Watercourse geometry comes from Ordnance Survey’s OS Open Rivers dataset rather than OpenStreetMap, since public Overpass API mirrors proved unreliable (repeated 504 timeouts) when queried for waterway features.

# OS Open Rivers (OGL/Crown copyright, free via OS Data Hub) - downloaded once
# and cached, since Overpass mirrors were unreliable for `waterway` queries.
rivers_zip <- file.path(cache_dir, "os_open_rivers_gb.gpkg")
rivers_extract_dir <- file.path(cache_dir, "os_open_rivers_extracted")
rivers_gpkg <- file.path(rivers_extract_dir, "Data", "oprvrs_gb.gpkg")

if (!file.exists(rivers_gpkg)) {
  if (!file.exists(rivers_zip)) {
    # download.file()/libcurl can trip sandboxes that block reading ~/.netrc;
    # disabling netrc lookup on the curl handle avoids that
    h <- curl::new_handle(netrc = 0, followlocation = TRUE, timeout = 600)
    curl::curl_download(
      "https://api.os.uk/downloads/v1/products/OpenRivers/downloads?area=GB&format=GeoPackage&redirect",
      destfile = rivers_zip, handle = h
    )
  }
  # The download is actually a zip containing the real .gpkg plus licence/readme docs
  unzip(rivers_zip, exdir = rivers_extract_dir)
}


bbox_bng <- st_bbox(st_transform(bbox_sf, 27700))

rivers_bng <- st_read(
  rivers_gpkg, layer = "watercourse_link",
  wkt_filter = st_as_text(st_as_sfc(bbox_bng)),
  quiet = TRUE
)

Within the same 10-mile radius, 590 watercourse segments are found, including named rivers and canals such as River Trent.

# Full-resolution shading (not the downsampled elmat_ds used for the plotly
# surface), since this feeds the 3D rayshader render below
hillshade <- elmat |>
  sphere_shade(texture = "imhof1") |>
  add_shadow(ray_shade(elmat, zscale = 30, multicore = TRUE), max_darken = 0.5) |>
  add_shadow(ambient_shade(elmat, zscale = 30), max_darken = 0.5)

river_overlay <- generate_line_overlay(
  rivers_bng, extent = ext_bng, heightmap = elmat,
  color = "steelblue4", linewidth = 3
)

hillshade_rivers <- add_overlay(hillshade, river_overlay)


snapshot_file <- file.path(cache_dir, "terrain_3d_rivers_snapshot.png")

rgl::close3d()
# zscale = 30 (cell size) / 5 exaggeration; at true scale (zscale = 30) or
# even 2x (zscale = 15) the ~415 m relief across a 30 km extent reads as
# nearly flat, so a stronger exaggeration and lower, more oblique phi make
# the terrain (and the rivers following its valleys) legible
plot_3d(
  hillshade_rivers, elmat,
  zscale = 6, windowsize = c(1000, 800),
  phi = 25, theta = 45, zoom = 0.6,
  solid = FALSE, shadowdepth = -50
)

zscale_3d <- 6

for (i in seq_len(nrow(top_peaks))) {
  # altitude is relative to the *local* terrain height (relativez = TRUE) and
  # gets stretched by zscale, so a modest +40 m keeps labels near the surface
  render_label(
    elmat, extent = ext_bng, zscale = zscale_3d,
    lat = top_peaks$northing[i], long = top_peaks$easting[i],
    altitude = 40, offset = 0,
    text = top_peaks$name[i], textsize = 1.1, linewidth = 2,
    clear_previous = (i == 1)
  )
}

render_label(
  elmat, extent = ext_bng, zscale = zscale_3d,
  lat = viewing_point$northing, long = viewing_point$easting,
  altitude = 50, offset = 0,
  text = viewing_point$name, textsize = 1.3, linewidth = 2,
  textcolor = "darkblue", linecolor = "darkblue"
)

render_label(
  elmat, extent = ext_bng, zscale = zscale_3d,
  lat = high_point$northing, long = high_point$easting,
  altitude = 40, offset = 0,
  text = sprintf("%s (%d m)", high_point$name, round(high_point$elev_dem)),
  textsize = 1.1, linewidth = 2,
  textcolor = "darkorange4", linecolor = "darkorange4"
)

Sys.sleep(3)
render_snapshot(filename = snapshot_file)
rgl::close3d()

knitr::include_graphics(snapshot_file)

title: Projecting the sun’s path for the 12 August 2026 UK partial solar eclipse
text:
Notes and caveats

Both photo overlays use a small-angle/linear projection from angular offset to pixel offset around the camera’s heading and pitch, rather than a true perspective (gnomonic) projection. This is a reasonable approximation for the field-of-view sizes and angular ranges involved here, but introduces increasing distortion toward the edges of wide fields of view.
The Street View camera’s field of view is assumed to be 90° both horizontally and vertically (the API default for a square image); the true vertical field of view for the Street View panorama projection may differ.
The photo’s field of view is estimated from its 35mm-equivalent focal length and an assumed native sensor resolution (4032x3024 for the iPhone 13 Pro Max ultra-wide camera), rescaled to the actual saved crop size. This is not a verified optical specification.
The photo’s pitch is taken directly from the Theodolite app’s vert_angle_deg caption field, and roll (horiz_angle_deg) is assumed negligible and not corrected for.
The terrain elevation data comes from AWS Terrain Tiles (~30m resolution) via elevatr. Named peaks are whichever natural=peak features happen to be tagged in OpenStreetMap within the radius — this list may be incomplete, and their elevations are read from the DEM at each point’s coordinates rather than from (often-missing) OSM elevation tags.
The river network is watercourse-link geometry from OS Open Rivers. Contains OS data © Crown copyright and database right, available under the Open Government Licence. It is a generalised network, not a detailed hydrography product, and roughly 200 of the segments in this radius carry no watercourse_name (minor streams/ditches).
Reprojecting the elevation raster from WGS84 to British National Grid leaves a small fraction (~2%) of edge cells as NA, visible as a faint ragged border in the 3D render.
The bounding box is built as a square in degrees (±10 miles in latitude and longitude), so its corners reach roughly 14 miles from the viewing location — farther than the stated 10-mile radius. The highest point in the frame (~381 m) falls in one such corner and is ~25 km from the nearest named OSM peak, so it is almost certainly real high ground (plausibly Peak District/Pennine foothills) rather than a labeling gap — OSM just has no natural=peak point there.

title: Instrumenting Agent Cybernetics
text:
Wang et al. (2026) argue that cybernetics supplies the missing theoretical scaffold for foundation agents, and derive six design principles from six classical laws. Their Principle 2 (Requisite Variety) requires that \(\min(V(\mathcal{O}), V(\mathcal{I})) \geq V(\mathcal{W})\), and three of the failure modes they name are diagnosed as \(V(\mathcal{T}) < V(\mathcal{W})\). Their headline open question — how should an agent respond when its environment exceeds its representational capacity? — presupposes that this condition can be detected.
It cannot, as the framework currently stands. \(V(\mathcal{W})\) appears throughout as Ashby’s classical cardinality — a theoretical quantity Wang et al. never operationalise from deployment telemetry. An operator who tries to estimate it from observed disturbance classes defaults to plug-in (maximum-likelihood) coverage; that default systematically understates environmental variety and overstates coverage, worst where the distribution is heaviest-tailed. Agent Cybernetics is, as written, unmeasurable.
We supply the instrument. Our central result is the Enumeration Elasticity Theorem: the elasticity of unhandled traffic with respect to enumeration investment is exactly \(\eta = 1 - \beta\), where \(\beta\) is the Heaps exponent of the disturbance-class discovery curve — a directly measurable quantity. A \(\lambda\)-fold increase in the effort spent mapping disturbance classes to responses reduces the unhandled fraction by \(\lambda^{1-\beta}\). As \(\beta \to 1\), \(\eta \to 0\) and investment stops buying coverage: at \(\beta = 0.9\), halving the residual costs a thousandfold increase in effort. This gives an operational answer to Wang et al.’s open question. When \(\eta \approx 0\), requisite variety cannot be met by amplification at any ledger a rational operator will build, and the deficit must be met by attenuation or by a class-independent fallback — an architectural conclusion, not an engineering one.
We further contribute: an open-world estimator for \(V(\mathcal{W})\) combining Good–Turing missing-mass correction and Heaps tracking, and a demonstration that plug-in estimation errs on both sides of the inequality at once; a determinism instrument, \(H(R \mid D)\), that operationalises the Conant–Ashby good regulator theorem, which is absent from the six laws; an interventional test that renders feedback blindness — a named closed-loop reliability failure they diagnose but do not measure (one of their first four failure modes, ranked highest for cost–benefit) — falsifiable rather than merely diagnosable, and which we run on the demonstrator (\(\Phi = 0.55\) bits, \(\approx\) 90x the resampling-noise floor: the agent’s action distribution genuinely conditions on its observations); and a partition-refinement procedure with three admission gates, including a policy-improvement criterion that corrects a natural but wrong instinct about when a disturbance class should be split.
We also identify a hazard in our own instrument: attenuation lowers measured \(\beta\), so the treatment we recommend improves the diagnostic whether or not it improves the system. We give the mitigation and do not claim to resolve it.
Finally, the same interventional machinery yields an adversarial instrument: susceptibility \(\Sigma\), the probability that an agent complies with an instruction injected into its observation channel (indirect prompt poisoning). Measured end-to-end through an agent’s real data-input tools — file read, RAG retrieval, web fetch — against a matched clean control (\(\Sigma_{\text{clean}} = 0\)), \(\Sigma\) is strongly attack-class-dependent (0.83 for a blunt instruction-override, 0.00 for a system-prompt-exfiltration attempt) and inversely tracks content-sensitivity \(\Phi\) across vectors, the direction §5.2 predicts: an agent that treats tool output as evidence to be checked, not an instruction to obey, is harder to hijack through that output, while a feedback-blind one passes an injected payload straight through.
We package these as a variety ledger: a versioned registry of essential variables, disturbance classes, response repertoire, and channel specifications, recomputed from telemetry and enforced as a CI gate. §6 exercises the full ledger on a semi-synthetic benchmark with known ground truth — including a graded outcome signal that makes the partition-refinement gates non-vacuous, an interventional feedback-blindness measurement, and an end-to-end prompt-poisoning susceptibility measurement — and reports one incident: a latent regulatory defect that inverted the dithering measurement until it was found and fixed, which is itself the clearest available demonstration of why §4.5’s canary discipline is not optional.

title: Instrumenting Agent Cybernetics
A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models
text:
Sclocchi, Favero and Wyart’s A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models Reveals the Hierarchical Nature of Data (Sclocchi, Favero, and Wyart 2024) makes a simple, sharp claim about how diffusion models generate images. Take a real image, run the forward noising process partway to some timestep \(t\), then run the backward (denoising) process the rest of the way back to \(t=0\). If \(t\) is small, you get back almost exactly the image you started with. If \(t\) is large, you get a plausible image of the same rough kind but with different fine details. The paper’s finding is that the switch between these two regimes isn’t gradual — it’s a genuine phase transition, and it happens at different noise levels for different levels of an image’s hierarchy (fine texture destabilizes first, then object parts, then overall semantic class).
This post reproduces that experiment end to end: real pretrained weights, real ImageNet-derived images, run locally on a Mac (Apple Silicon, no CUDA) rather than the multi-GPU cluster the paper used. The code lives in forward-backward-diffusion, the paper’s own release — I had to fix a couple of bugs in it and add Apple GPU (MPS) support to get it running here; the how and why of that is at the bottom of the post.

title: A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models
section: Scaling it down to run on a laptop
text:
Scaling it down to run on a laptop
The paper’s own experiment uses OpenAI’s 256×256 unconditional ADM diffusion model over the full ImageNet-1k validation set (1000 classes, 10 images each), resampled to 250 diffusion steps, swept across the full 0–250 range of reversal points. Doing that on a single Mac would take a very long time, so this reproduction keeps every piece of the pipeline real but turns the dials down:




Paper
This post




Diffusion model
256×256 unconditional ADM (OpenAI)
same checkpoint


Classifier
ConvNeXt-Base (torchvision, ImageNet-1k)
same model


Images
ImageNet-1k validation, 1000 classes × 10
Imagenette validation, 10 classes × 3 (a real, license-free ImageNet subset)


Diffusion steps (respaced)
250
25


Reversal points swept
0–250 (fine grid)
7 points: 3, 6, 10, 14, 18, 22, 25


Hardware
GPU cluster
Apple M4 Pro, MPS backend, fp32



So: same model, same classifier, same underlying mechanism, real (if smaller) ImageNet-derived data — just a coarser grid and a tenth-scale image set, sized to finish in about 20 minutes on a laptop instead of hours on a cluster.

title: A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models
section: Where does the class identity break?
text:
Where does the class identity break?
For each reversal point \(t\), we forward-diffuse every starting image to \(t\), denoise it back to a clean image, and ask ConvNeXt-Base what class it thinks the result is — then compare that to what it originally said about the untouched image. sample_correct and start_correct track agreement with the true (Imagenette) label; pred_unchanged tracks whether reconstruction preserved the classifier’s own original prediction, which is the more direct read on “did the reverse process preserve identity” independent of whether the classifier was right to begin with.

summary_by_t <- accuracy_by_t |>
  group_by(step_reverse) |>
  summarise(
    sample_correct = mean(sample_correct),
    pred_unchanged = mean(pred_unchanged),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(c(sample_correct, pred_unchanged), names_to = "metric", values_to = "fraction")

baseline_acc <- baseline$accuracy_top1[1] / 100

ggplot(summary_by_t, aes(step_reverse, fraction, color = metric)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = baseline_acc, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  annotate("text", x = max(summary_by_t$step_reverse), y = baseline_acc,
           label = "baseline accuracy (no diffusion)", vjust = -0.6, hjust = 1,
           size = 3, color = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(sample_correct = "#2C7FB8", pred_unchanged = "#D95F02"),
    labels = c(sample_correct = "matches true label", pred_unchanged = "matches original prediction")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "reversal timestep (t, out of 25 respaced steps)",
    y = "fraction of images",
    color = NULL,
    title = "Identity survives small t, then degrades"
  )







Figure 1: Classification agreement after forward-backward diffusion, as a function of the reversal timestep. t=0 is a no-op (perfect reconstruction); higher t means more of the diffusion trajectory is re-randomized before reconstruction.

title: A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models
section: A hierarchy of breakdown, layer by layer
text:
A hierarchy of breakdown, layer by layer
The more interesting view is inside the classifier. Every image gets pushed through ConvNeXt-Base twice — once as the original, once as the forward-backward reconstruction — and we compare activations at every one of its ~45 internal layers, from the earliest convolutional stem (depth 0) to the final classification head (depth ≈44). If the paper’s hierarchical story is right, shallow layers (fine texture) should start diverging at small \(t\), while only the deepest layers (semantic class) diverge at large \(t\).

cosine_by_depth_t <- activation_diff |>
  filter(metric == "cosine") |>
  group_by(step_reverse, depth) |>
  summarise(cosine_distance = 1 - mean(value), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(cosine_by_depth_t, aes(step_reverse, depth, fill = cosine_distance)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", labels = percent_format()) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = pretty_breaks()) +
  labs(
    x = "reversal timestep (t)",
    y = "network depth (0 = input stem, ~44 = classification head)",
    fill = "cosine\ndistance",
    title = "Where in the network reconstruction diverges from the original"
  )







Figure 2: Mean cosine distance (1 - cosine similarity) between original and reconstructed activations, by network depth and reversal timestep. Warmer = more disrupted. A hierarchy would show the disruption front moving from shallow layers (bottom) to deep layers (top) as t increases.






depth_max <- max(cosine_by_depth_t$depth)
sample_depths <- unique(round(seq(0, depth_max, length.out = 6)))

cosine_by_depth_t |>
  filter(depth %in% sample_depths) |>
  mutate(depth = factor(depth)) |>
  ggplot(aes(step_reverse, cosine_distance, color = depth, group = depth)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "magma", end = 0.85) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) +
  labs(
    x = "reversal timestep (t)",
    y = "cosine distance",
    color = "depth",
    title = "Shallow layers move first, deep layers move last"
  )







Figure 3: The same data as a line plot: a handful of representative depths, cosine distance vs. t.

title: A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models
A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models
section: What actually broke in the code, and how I fixed it
text:
What actually broke in the code, and how I fixed it
The paper’s released code isn’t quite runnable as committed, and separately, nothing about it was written with Apple’s MPS backend in mind. Four fixes were needed:

A broken relative import. guided_diffusion/image_datasets.py did from ..datasets.imagenet_classes import IMAGENET_CLASSES, a relative import that reaches outside the installed guided_diffusion package. It fails immediately with ImportError: attempted relative import beyond top-level package — every one of the repo’s three custom scripts imports this module, so nothing in the repo could run at all. Fixed by making datasets its own installable package (setup.py) and importing it absolutely.
Two sampling methods that don’t exist. The actual forward-backward experiment script calls diffusion.p_sample_loop_forw_back and diffusion.ddim_sample_loop_forw_back — methods that appear nowhere in gaussian_diffusion.py, and never have, across the entire git history. I implemented both, as variants of the existing p_sample_loop_progressive / ddim_sample_loop_progressive that start the reverse process at a given timestep instead of at pure noise.
float64 on MPS. _extract_into_tensor moved the diffusion schedule’s coefficients — stored as float64 numpy arrays — directly onto the compute device. MPS doesn’t support float64 at all, so this crashed on first use; fixed by casting to float32 before the device transfer.
torch.distributed collectives on an MPS tensor. The scripts use dist.all_reduce/all_gather (inherited from the original multi-GPU design) even for a single-process laptop run. Those collectives run over the gloo backend here (no CUDA means no NCCL), and gloo only understands CPU tensors — so the handful of tensors that cross a collective call needed to be routed to CPU rather than MPS, while leaving NCCL’s CUDA path untouched for the cluster case.

None of this changes the paper’s method — it’s the same forward-then-partial-backward diffusion process, the same classifier, the same activation-comparison logic. The fixes just make the released code actually executable, and executable somewhere other than a CUDA cluster.

title: A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models
text:
References
